title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) nonempty for every \(n\ge 1\), does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in \(1/\varepsilon\), independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-\(\varepsilon\) distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
definitions: \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a nonempty subset of graphs on \([n]\), invariant under vertex permutations. For \(n\ge 2, \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})=\min _{H\in \mathrm{P}_{n}}|E(G)\triangle E(H)|/\operatorname{binom}(n,2)\); for \(n=1\) it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer \(t\ge 2\), with \(\varepsilon =1/t\), and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each \(G\in \mathrm{P}_{n}\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\) and rejects each G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})\ge \varepsilon\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\); no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants \(C,a\ge 1\) with at most \(Ct^{a}\) adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants \(C' ,b\ge 1\), using at most \(C' t^{b}\) queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with \(\Pr [|q- \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})|\le 1/t]\ge 2/3\) for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

progress.text: Fischer and Newman prove a general tester-to-estimator conversion with a large quantitative overhead, leaving the polynomial regime open.
Gishboliner, Kushnir and Shapira revisit testing versus estimation and improve general conversion bounds, but do not obtain the conjectured polynomial transformation.
Gishboliner and Shapira state Problem 5.4: decide whether \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\varepsilon )\) testability implies estimation with \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) sample complexity.

status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The cited survey still states the polynomial tester-to-estimator implication as open; known conversions and positive special cases do not establish the universal claim.
review_note: The former short index record is upgraded to the precise Problem 5.4 formulation from the 2025 survey. The exponent c is a normalization of \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\); the dense-model distance and query quantifiers are explicit.

context_blocks.text: Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are \(\varepsilon\)-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on \(\varepsilon\). The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\varepsilon )\) can be replaced by \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.

sentences: A dense-graph tester queries adjacencies to distinguish membership in a property from graphs far from it.
A distance estimator instead approximates the minimum fraction of edge changes needed to reach that property.
The question asks whether a query bound polynomial in inverse accuracy for testing always entails such a polynomial bound for estimation.
Each algorithm is uniform and the query bound is independent of graph size, while local computation is unrestricted.
This card isolates the polynomial implication in its title from the stronger quantitative conversion posed in the cited survey.
